item.text:
**5B.1 Research Note**
Kishida’s 2024 record is **mostly consistent with broad-based, sustainable prosperity rather than rent extraction or pure popularity-seeking**, but it was weakened by the LDP funding scandal and by repeated signs that political survival and popularity pressures mattered. The strongest positive evidence is his wage-growth agenda, child-support expansion, regional subsidies, and refusal to continue faction politics. The strongest negatives are the scandal itself and reporting that he was under pressure to save popularity and manage coalition politics.

- [Policy Speech by Prime Minister Kishida to the 213th Session of the Diet](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202401/30shiseihoshin.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | January 30, 2024 | Kishida made wage increases, child support, and cost-of-living relief the core of his 2024 agenda, and said funding would come through spending reform rather than new burdens on the public. This is strong evidence for broad-based, long-term prosperity aims. | Question IDs: 5B.1

- [Press Conference by Prime Minister Kishida](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/statement/202406/21kaiken.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | June 21, 2024 | Kishida said broad subsidies would cushion low-income households, families, agriculture, SMEs, care services, childcare, schools, transit, logistics, and regional tourism from price spikes. This is direct evidence of trying to spread gains broadly rather than concentrate them. | Question IDs: 5B.1, 4B.7

- [Meeting of the Council on Economic and Fiscal Policy](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/actions/202404/19keizai.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | April 19, 2024 | Kishida tied regional revitalization to national development and said local communities need sustainable administrative services, digital tools, and grants. This supports a reading of prosperity strategy that is geographically broad and not just Tokyo-centered. | Question IDs: 5B.1, 4B.7, 4B.4

- [May 2024 actions index](https://japan.kantei.go.jp/101_kishida/actions/202405/index.html) | Prime Minister’s Office of Japan | May 2024 | The Prime Minister’s Office grouped Kishida’s agenda around wage increases, growth strategy, digital administration, distribution strategy, and child support. This is a policy-menu signal that the administration was trying to build a durable growth-and-redistribution package. | Question IDs: 5B.1

- [Japan PM Kishida sets eye on wage rises as focus of 'new capitalism'](https://www.investing.com/news/economy/japan-pm-kishida-sets-eye-on-wage-rises-as-focus-of-new-capitalism-3043660) | Reuters | March 29, 2023 | Reuters described Kishida’s “new capitalism” as focusing on wage increases, innovation, reskilling, labor mobility, and support for startups, explicitly because there is no growth without redistribution. This is older context, but it directly informs how his 2024 economic program was framed. | Question IDs: 5B.1

- [Japan's chief cabinet secretary calls for broad-based wage hikes](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/japans-chief-cabinet-secretary-calls-for-broadbased-wage-hikes-3530320) | Reuters | July 23, 2024 | Reuters said broadening pay hikes among smaller firms was crucial and that rising wages were a policy priority to prevent inflation from hurting consumption and recovery. This supports the view that the administration sought sustainable, demand-led prosperity rather than short-term political patronage. | Question IDs: 5B.1

- [Embattled Japan PM faces ethics committee, with popularity and budget on the line](https://www.investing.com/news/economy/embattled-japan-pm-faces-ethics-committee-to-save-popularity-and-budget-3319362) | Reuters | February 28, 2024 | Reuters reported Kishida appeared before a parliamentary ethics committee to contain the funding scandal, and that the episode hurt his popularity and could delay the budget. This is negative evidence: political survival and reputational repair were clearly in play. | Question IDs: 5B.1, 4B.2, 4B.10

- [Japan PM steps down amid scandals and weak support](https://www.investing.com/news/economy-news/japan-pm-kishida-wont-run-for-reelection-at-ldp-race-kyodo-reports-3570455) | Reuters | August 14, 2024 | Reuters framed Kishida’s exit as driven by public disaffection over scandals and living costs, and Kishida said stepping aside was the first step to show the LDP was changing. This is mixed evidence: it shows responsiveness and some reform intent, but also confirms politics and popularity were central constraints. | Question IDs: 5B.1, 4B.10, 4B.8

- [Analysis: Japan's Kishida championed 'new capitalism' but was undone by yen](https://www.thestar.com.my/news/world/2024/08/14/analysis-japan039s-kishida-championed-039new-capitalism039-but-was-undone-by-yen) | Reuters | August 14, 2024 | Reuters said Kishida pushed through some of Japan’s biggest wage increases in decades, but weak purchasing power and scandals still undercut him politically. This is supportive on substance, but it also shows the prosperity program did not fully translate into durable political payoff. | Question IDs: 5B.1

- [AP report on Kishida’s political compromise](https://apnews.com/article/05926b50f4f5a83a631f779d906cf06d) | Associated Press | September 30, 2024 | AP said Kishida compromised with conservative nationalists to stay in power. That is mixed evidence: it suggests coalition maintenance and survival politics, but not obvious rent extraction or a pure popularity-maximizing style. | Question IDs: 5B.1, 4B.8, 4B.10

**Search gap**
I did not find credible evidence that Kishida used 2024 policy primarily to extract rents or buy loyalty. The negative evidence is mostly about scandal, coalition management, and popularity pressure, not outright predation.
